newsitem.title: UK: UK's Blair and Major come out fighting on final day.
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair and Major come out fighting on final day.

text.p: Despite polls promising him a landslide victory, Tony Blair's Labour Party planned a last minute blitz on the final day of Britain's election campaign on Wednesday and Prime Minister John Major insisted he could still win.
As the gruelling six-week campaign edged toward a close and two polls gave Labour 18 and 20 percent leads, Blair said on Tuesday he was taking nothing for granted.

A Gallup poll for ITN Channel 4 News showed Labour 18 points ahead of the ruling Conservatives. A poll in the Daily Telegraph gave them a 20 point lead and a projected majority of 203 parliamentary seats, which would be the biggest margin for any party since 1832.
Looking increasing assured, Blair urged 500 rapturous supporters at a rally in Bristol, southwest England, on Tuesday to show their support for Labour with their votes on Thursday.

Invoking the memory of former Labour Party leader John Smith, whose sudden death from a heart attack in 1994 led to Blair taking over the party leadership and launching its radical overhaul, Blair said he would always remember what Smith said the night before he died.
"All we ask is the chance to serve." he said.
"And that's what we ask of the British people in the next two days. All we ask is the chance to serve. We believe we can make this country better," Blair continued.

Labour planned to make the most of the final day of the campaign. Full-page advertisements warning voters of the "cost of voting Conservative" appeared in British newspapers and half a million supporters were set to work to get people out to vote on Thursday.

Major was also in fighting spirit on Tuesday when he warned that May 1 would be "a day of destiny" for the British people. He insisted that unless the Conservatives were returned for a fifth consecutive term the country would change for the worse.

"This election is about the unity of the United Kingdom. It is, literally, a battle for Britain...If we lose, Britain will change, yes -- change forever, change for the worse," he told 2,000 supporters at a London rally.
Insisting that the opinion polls, which have consistently put Labour ahead, could not be trusted, Major said the Conservatives still had a chance for victory.
"I think this election is there to be won. There are a lot of people who are undecided," he said in a television interview.
"I am rather dismissive of opinion polls, they were proved wrong in the last election and I believe they will be proved wrong in this one," he said.

Earlier on Tuesday Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine told voters they would be "sleepwalking into a nightmare" by voting Labour and predicted the Conservatives would win with a majority of more than 60 seats.
Responding to Heseltine's comments, Blair said: "The disaster is a Tory fifth term."
